Method, assumptions & sources
  • Compression = (cross-section − gland depth) / cross-section. The worst case combines the O-ring cross-section tolerance, the gland tolerances and the installed stretch. Optionally the parts are fully offset by the radial clearance (eccentricity).
  • Stretch flattens the cross-section; the reduction follows Parker's empirical curve (ORD 5700, fig. 3-3). Piston grooves: stretch on the groove bottom. Rod grooves: stretch on the rod, or circumferential compression of the centreline. Face grooves: the O-ring should seat on the outer wall for internal pressure and on the inner wall for external pressure.
  • Gland fill = installed cross-section area / gland area (bottom radii removed); volume is conserved when the ring is stretched. Hot fill adds the O-ring's volumetric thermal expansion and the volume swell; the metal is assumed not to expand (conservative).
  • Rounded rectangles: perimeter = 2(L + W) − (8 − 2π)R. Stretch and fit compare O-ring and groove perimeters. A centreline corner radius of at least 3 × cross-section is a common rule of thumb.
  • Dovetail grooves: gland area = depth × opening width + depth² · tan(undercut angle); the O-ring mean diameter should match the groove mean diameter (Parker Design Chart 4-4, ERIKS Table 3.C-3). Boss seals: AS568 -9xx rings with port and MS33656 fitting-end dimensions from the ERIKS handbook; the check covers the stretch on the fitting undercut and the material limits.
  • Guidelines: Parker ORD 5700 Design Tables 4-2 (industrial static), 4-3 (face seals), 5-2 and 5-2-b (industrial reciprocating, inch and metric); ERIKS O-ring Technical Handbook section 12 Tables 3.C-1 (face, metric), 3.C-2 (static radial, metric), 3.D-1 (dynamic, metric), 3.D-2 (back-up rings) and 3.B-1a (clearance). Other cross-sections are interpolated from these tables.
  • Limits used: static compression 12–30 % (max. 30 %, Parker), dynamic 8–16 %; minimum squeeze ≈ 0.2 mm; gland fill 60–85 % nominal, optimum 75 %, at least 10 % void; installed stretch ≤ 5 % (Parker), ≤ 3 % for face seals (ERIKS); clearances halved for silicone and fluorosilicone; back-up rings above 103.5 bar static (Parker) or 50 bar dynamic (ERIKS).
  • Sizes: AS568 dimensions per AS568A as listed in Parker ORD 5700 Table 9-1; ISO 3601-1 series G per Parker Table 9-6. Material temperature ranges and expansion coefficients are typical values (Parker Table 2-5).
  • Not covered: rotary seals, pneumatic floating rings, crush seals, friction and assembly force, extrusion charts versus pressure and hardness, thermal expansion of the housing. Design guides are guidelines; confirm with the seal supplier.

O-Ring Groove Designer

Version 1.2 · by Eren Tozlu

A free, browser-based tool for designing and checking O-ring grooves (glands): piston and rod seals, static or dynamic, and face seals with circular or rounded-rectangle grooves. It checks compression with worst-case tolerances, gland fill, stretch, extrusion gap, temperature and material limits. All calculations run in your browser.

Includes the AS568 and ISO 3601-1 size series, an elastomer library and groove guideline tables based on the public design guides of Parker (O-Ring Handbook ORD 5700) and ERIKS (O-ring Technical Handbook). Not affiliated with or endorsed by these companies.

Made by Eren Tozlu. More engineering tools and projects at ehcrea.com.

How to use the O-Ring Groove Designer

New here? Pick an example from Load application example… in the toolbar, then change one value at a time and watch the results.

Four steps

  1. Application: choose the seal type. Piston: groove in the inner part, sealing against a bore. Rod: groove in the housing, sealing against a rod or shaft. Face: groove in a flat face under a cover. Dovetail: undercut face groove that holds the O-ring. Boss port: O-ring of a straight-thread tube fitting. Then set static or dynamic motion, the pressure direction (face seals) and the groove outline: circle or rounded rectangle.
  2. O-ring: pick a standard size (AS568, ISO 3601-1 or boss seals) or enter a custom one, then the material and hardness. Suggest O-ring picks the standard size that fits your hardware best.
  3. Hardware & groove: enter the main dimension (bore, rod, groove wall or centreline) and press Apply recommended groove to size the groove from the Parker or ERIKS guideline. Adjust the dimensions and tolerances to match your drawing.
  4. Operating conditions: pressure, temperature range and the volume swell of the O-ring in your fluid.

The gland

Gland depth L
Distance from the groove bottom to the mating surface; for radial seals it includes the radial clearance, for face seals the flange gap.
Groove width G
Room for the O-ring to deform sideways, for swell and for back-up rings.
Clearance E
Diametral gap between the moving or mating parts (E/2 per side): the extrusion path under pressure.
Compression (squeeze)
(CS − L) / CS: how much the cross-section is squeezed. Too little leaks, too much causes high friction, compression set and damage. Static 12–30 %, dynamic 8–16 %.
Gland fill
O-ring cross-section area / gland area. Aim for about 75 % and stay below 85 %, so there is room for swell and thermal expansion.
Stretch
How much the O-ring ID is stretched at installation. Keep below 5 % (3 % for face seals); stretch also flattens the cross-section.
Worst case
All tolerances at their least favourable limits: the smallest ring in the deepest gland, and the other way round.

Reading the results

  • The badge shows OK, Check (warnings) or Problem (errors). Each warning says what to change.
  • Recommended groove compares your design with the guideline values; ✓ is within the guideline, ! is outside.
  • The libraries at the bottom list all O-ring sizes, the groove guideline tables and the materials. Click a row to use it.
  • The ⓘ icons explain individual inputs. Copy link saves the whole design in a link; Unit converter converts lengths, pressures and temperatures.

The tool follows the public design guides of Parker and ERIKS. Always confirm critical seals with the seal supplier and by testing.
